review:
I recently just got this game to play with my 4 year old son.  We love split screen and local coop games so I wanted to leave a review here for anybody who was on the fence about this game!

Gameplay: 8
Combat is easy and intuitive to learn even for my son's age group.  The crafting system is more complex than the menus of Minecraft but he was able to get used to it rather quickly.  This game is a nice blend of a dungeon crawler RPG and Minecraft builder elements.  The worlds to explore are beautifully lit but sometimes it can be dark to see at night until you find reliable light sources.

Controls: 10
Everything works great here.  It is really easy to assign items to the hotbar, access your various menu/crafting screens, and combat flows smoothly.  We both used controllers while playing the game on PC and were able to splitscreen perfectly fine using both.  

Story: 7
Does not seem to be too deep of a story here but that is the nature of a game like this.  The objective is simple to continue crafting, improving your character, and progressing to harder worlds through the portals.

Graphics: 8
The art is beautiful in this game and the animations all work nicely.  The only downside is the there is no option to adjust your gamma settings so night time can be extremely dark if you do not have torches or lanterns around.

Overall: 8
Reccomend this game to anybody looking for a fun experience filled with loot, leveling up, bosses, exploration, and crafting.  Coop mode is excellent!

After several hours of playing Portal Knights from time to time, i think i can give a decent review for you.
The first thing i wanna say is: PK is a really good game and has the potential to be one of the best sandbox RPG's out there, but lacks some RPG content and other things i am going to tell you.

Pros:

- The graphic of PK is imo very beautiful and fresh.
- animations (characters and enemies) are fluid and nearly every enemy has it's own mechanics and fighting style. The game get's easier while you learn the diffrent patterns
- The character customization is O.K. (race (with Elves DLC), gender, hair, eyes, voice, colors, ears, accessiors...).
- 3 unique classes (+1 with Rogue DLC) all with unique skills and abilities
- The weapon- and armor skins are decent looking and have a cool design.
- ability to customize your characters without losing armor stats - you wanna be a warrior in a rabbit costume? go for it! you wanna wear that cool magearmor on your warrior? feel free to do it!
- various weapon types for the different classes
- various different biomes, with totally different appearance
- selectable island size
- harvesting 
- NPC's and merchants you can relocate
- simple but well implemented quests and questlines
- vacant islands with no monsters for building.
- possibility to reset your world for new content without loosing your progress on vacant-/home islands.
- creative mode with unlimited blocks and designable islands.
- unlimited building possibilies, with lots of unique blocks.
- many, very cool and unique decoration items to customize your home.
- the crafting system is O.K. could be better though.
- developers listen to community, good bug support, new updates every few months. 
- 4 man coop mode
- Hardmode bosses and lategame instances (Rift's with DLC) may be challanging even for good players
- anti griefing mechanic allows you to decide if people can build/loot chests on your home islands
- DLC's (some are free, some are a bit overpriced, Rogue&Rift DLC totally worth it, if you enjoy the game)
- seasonal events

For the cons i firstly wanna say, that the RPG content in PK could be way better.
The balance of classes, weapons, skill points, spells is really bad. Why go for a melee weapon, if you can deal nearly the same damage with a ranged weapon?
There is a great weapon variation, but in the end there are only 1-2 types per class to go for. The talents you can trait after leveling your character should get a rework, because some of them are just useless.

Cons:

- every enemy in PK will hit you like a rock, means you will die within 2-3 hits if not investing skillpoints in health. This might be a challange for some players, but can be frustrating.
- ranged combat feels much more rewarding than melee combat
- as melee: prepare to die - alot
- classes are a bit unbalanced in difficulty (warrior is very easy for beginners, as mage you will run mostly and try to not get hit by anything. Also spells are a bit weak, consume a lot of mana)
- combat quickly gets boring and annoying because no attack variations
- no coin storage possible (this sucks because everytime you die you loose 100 coins)
- dodgeroll 80% of time 
- water is in the game but no swimming or diving, just lower gravity. Some enemys don't drown in water, but you do.
- most of the random events feel clunky - 90% go there, kill this trashmob X-times
- level grind from lv. 25-30 because PK is lacking late game content. Means you have to kill bosses or monsters over and over again or reset your world and repeat quests
- after lv. 30 there is not much to go for RPG wise - you maybe wanna get steam achievments or optimize your characters armor
- hard mode bosses are really difficult solo, but pretty doable in coop-mode
- many items dropped by monsters are simply useless and after some time you will constantly delete stuff filling your inventory
- many items to harvest are mostly useless because you can buy all the important stuff from vendors (potions, ...)
- no instanced loot in coop - who picks it up first, keeps it

Conclusion:

BUY if you are into building/collecting/adventuring. Buy on sale if you are interested in this game.

To be completely honest, I think this game is extremely monotonous, don't let my thumbs up fool you. I put over 100 hours into this game and I enjoyed it for what it was (thanks to the massive amount of patience I have), but the biggest problem with this game is that there isn't anything to do really, which is hindering this game from being a solid competitor to giants like Minecraft or Terraria. You jump from world to world trying to find the next portal and you quickly begin to realize that they all look the same and none of them have much to offer other than to mine, fight nearly the same enemies over and over, explore petty dungeons, and find the next portal. The game isn't as deep as a game like Terraria for example and honestly I wonder if this game is meant for kids or something. Let me make a simple pros/cons list.

Pros:
-  Game feels really well made, very polished, no bugs, no crashes.
-  Graphics are surprisingly amazing for such a simple game. Very pretty to look at.
-  Combat is simple, yet very fluid and fun.
-  The game has a leveling system (1-30), points to spend on stats and you get passives. Has a sense of progression.
-  Create your own character. Character customization.
-  Pretty cool crafting system, nothing deep but still fun.
-  You can build things of course.
-  Tons of loot.
-  Has little events you can complete for special rewards sometimes. Holiday events, etc.
-  The music is amazing.
-  Up to 3 friends can join your game anytime they want and play with you. Has local Co-op.

Cons:
-  Only 3 bosses (and 3 hard mode versions of those bosses I believe).
-  Needs more NPC's on each world, and they need to give more quests.
-  Needs a larger variety of enemies.
-  Needs more unique worlds, as the game seems to only have about 10 or more biomes with 47 worlds to explore, so you can imagine how that plays out.
-  Needs more classes, only has Warrior, Ranger, and Mage. It's not a big deal, but I think at least 2 more could've been thrown in there.
-  Get's repetitive really fast, biggest reason being because of lack of content.

The reason I gave this game a thumbs up are for 2 reasons. One, because it did keep me occupied for a solid 100+ hours so I think it'd be dumb to give it a thumbs down really. And Two, I really hope the developers are reading this and add a lot more things to do in this game, because I honestly feel that is one of the only things holding this game back in my opinion. Other than that the game is addicting. Don't go into this game expecting a ton of sh*t to do and you'll be fine.
Very fun game for an awesome gaming father to play with their awesome 9 yr old daughter.

Portal Knights is a cute light RPG sandbox, with building and crafting.
It's playable alone, in co-op through steam or dedicated server (didn't try the last option, it's pretty new!). The game is cute, well polished and more importantly fun!

You explore islands procedurally generated (44 more - they added more of them with festivals and updates!), with different biomes, random dungeons, random quests (mostly to get more xp or unique furniture) and random events, gather new ressources to craft better armor or weapons, but also furniture for your home.
You don't "need" to build a home base but you'll quickly want to do it to gather more ressources. And also for the sake of building, it's fun, that's all.
Controls are easy and pleasant to use (some won't like the auto target thing, but you can disable it in the options).

There is enough content to keep you on the game at  least 30h. Way more if you really dig the genre. You can safely buy the game, it's really worth the price asked.

But, don't buy this game if:
- you want an openworld game. It's not.
- you want a strong RPG game. You'll find only 3 classes to choose from. They don't make a lot of  difference, the RPG  features are very light and won't appeal to someone looking for a deep combat or customisation system.
- you want a very difficult game. There is some end game stuff (hard mode bosses), but it's mainly a casual game (casual can be fun too!).

If those points don't turn you away, the game is just a gem, buy it.

The short version of this review is that this game is fun but definitely not for everyone so be mindful of the kind of games you like to play.  Portal Knights is a mix between a Sandbox and an RPG/Adventure type of game but all the aspects of each genre are watered down a bit.  If you can handle that, then Portal Knights might be worth a try. 

As for the long version, keep reading.

A few of my friends and I got this game on PS4 when it was free with Playstation Plus a few years ago.  Played it almost non-stop for a few days so my hours played on steam doesn't reflect my total time playing the actual game.

To sum up this game, it's as if Minecraft and Legend of Zelda had a child then when that child hit puberty, Skyrim and WoW came along and gave it a few tips.  Portal Knights then grew up to have several aspects of each of these games but to a lesser extent.  

---Let's start with the building---

The building and digging is voxel-based like Minecraft but is it as good as Minecraft?  No.  The building does allow players to use various blocks and furniture items to create amazing structures.  However, it doesn't have as many blocks as Minecraft, it doesn't have anything akin to redstone items and sometimes the building can be finicky.  Although, credit where credit is due, Portal Knights has some quality of life to its building and mining such as being able to place blocks at a much greater distance and having the ability to use a drill to dig up multiple blocks at once.  There are also islands which you can purchase that are huge, flat and perfect for building.

---Now for the Adventure/Combat---

Portal Knights does have a story.  It's a cute story and it kind of gives you an explanation as to why its universe is the way it is.  Obviously it's not going to leave your heart pounding and most of it is told through text but it's not too lengthy.  The world is segmented into different maps, most of which require you to find a portal and turn it on in order to progress and a lot of worlds have multiple portals.  The worlds are varied with later worlds being drastically different from the ones you first start out in.  There are typically dungeons or mines in each world which will often have chests full of treasure in them.  Money, gear, consumables and unique items can be found in these chests and the more difficult the world, the better the loot. This aspect might be a hit or miss for some people because worlds are somewhat broken up by loading screens and once you've explored them they lose a bit of their appeal.  Traversing some of these maps can also be a chore, especially if you need to build a long bridge to get to where you need to go.

There are also quests that reward XP, money and items on occasion.  Some are required to progress the game and are fairly easy to complete.  Some text will tell you about the story but most quests are usually "go kill these enemies," "bring me this item," or "place this item here."  Though sometimes there are NPCs that will be available for you to bring back to your home, some of which are merchants that will sell you useful items.

Combat is a bit like Legend of Zelda in that you lock onto a target and attack with your weapon.  You can also dodge roll to get out of the way when attacked.  It's neither the best nor the worst combat system I've experienced.  Though some aspects can be annoying, most notably the camera.  The camera isn't always in the best position when you need to fight something in a tight space.  Early enemies are pretty easy to take out but most enemies have strengths and weaknesses which will be useful on more difficult enemies later in the game.  It's mostly the bosses that require fancy footwork, though.  The first few bosses aren't going to give you too much trouble but when you start getting into the really hard ones, they'll give you a run for your money and then some.  Each class plays differently though not drastically.  Interestingly, all classes can use spells.  A warrior might not have enough mana to cast more that one or two fireballs but it's an option if you want it.

---Throw in some RPG---

Probably the most interesting thing about Portal Knights is that when creating a character, you pick a class just like in a RPG.  Warrior, Ranger and Mage are the three original choices with Rogue and Druid being available through DLC.  Each class has a different style of fighting enemies.  Along with this class system, you also level up.  Each time you level up you are awarded with points to spend in attributes which can increase your health, mana, physical damage, magical damage, etc.  Classes also gain more health and mana naturally as they level, with or without spending points into attributes that also increase those stats.  There is a potion you can make to reset these attribute points should you want to redistribute them.

Another thing that unlocks as you level is the skill tree.  Typically every five or so levels, you unlock another set of skills to choose from.  Each class gets a skill tree unique to their class.  Some skills are more useful during normal gameplay while others are more useful in boss fights.  Only one skill per tier can be active at a time but you can switch between them as long as you're not in combat.

These RPG aspects give the game a bit of flavor.  Whether or not you like that particular flavor is up to you.  Each class needs different things in order to progress.  A warrior needs an anvil to make better weapons and armor while a ranger needs an archer's station to make their version of upgrades and a mage will need an altar to craft their spells.  The greater the item, the greater the materials you need.  The crafting stations themselves also need to be upgraded to progress to the next tier of items.  You naturally run into these resources as you progress through the worlds.

---Best played with friends---

As with most games, friends make the experience more enjoyable.  There are bosses in this game that are difficult to take down without a group and having some people you can trust is always great.  But even if you do bring in strangers, there are some settings you can change to make sure they can't grief your world.

---Mostly Kid Friendly---

The controls might be a bit difficult for young children to get used to but other than that, there's no profanity, no gore, no overly violent themes or anything like that.  Portal Knights is rated E10+ and I'm inclined to agree.

---In Conclusion---

Portal Knights is an interesting take on the Sandbox genre.  It's not going to appeal to everyone, not by a long shot.  But there are some people who will absolutely love this game.  If you've read this entire review and are still having trouble deciding if it's worth buying, then it might be best to wait until it's on sale before purchasing.

Summary: 
This is a great game for ages 7 to 14 and seems to be best played as a multiplayer with friends or family.  I played this with my two kids who fall in that age range and they loved it.  I myself, having a lot more game experience felt the game lacked that "certain something" that makes so many other games addictive.

Pros: the graphics are fun and the game does not feel like a grind.  There is a story line although if you want to fully experience the story, I suggest playing it as a single player as in a multiplayer, you'll miss out on a lot if you're not the one interacting with the many NPC's.  Bosses can be re-spawned so this too is a plus if you miss out on a major battle. The portals mean that travel is quick and painless.  The fighting mechanics are fun and intuitive, especially if you've played a fair amount of zelda or other 3rd person perspective games with targeting systems. I played as the Ranger and was able to avoid almost all damage.

Cons: the game feels repetitive after the first area. By this I mean that you're basically following the same steps to explore, upgrade and fight, but simply with a different set of minerals/blocks to find which result in a different set of gear.  It's difficult to get OP items which I see as neither good or bad. Following the basic story line feels a bit mundane to me.

There is really not a lot of "exploration". We played on a "Large" world, which is the medium setting and it felt pretty small to me.  It should be mentioned that the previous game we all were playing was Minecraft which is just about infinite.  This game follows a very similar mine/craft/build mechanic, but it somehow lacks that immersive feel.

What I'd change: Death in this game lacks enough consequences for me to worry about dying at all. If dying is not a big deal, it sort of takes away the excitement.  Thus, I pretty much got board about 1/2 way through the game.
Resources are also too easy to obtain. Finding ores or gems never felt exciting. Dungeons are too easy.

Summary: Game is to easy for veteran gamers and while not feeling grindy, it did feel repetitive and lacks the overall excitement I felt in similar games.  It's too bad the developers abandon this as I think these issues could have been resolved with a few simple tweaks like adding different difficulty modes. which would have made resources less common, mobs more common and death more detrimental.

Recommended for newer gamers, who want a more casual forgiving and fun experience.

The basics
Three classes, Ive only tried the Mage/Wizard class so far. So, I cant speak of the other classes. However, Ive died a few times. Mistakes happen. It takes a minute or two just to get used to the combat camera. Once you get over that little hump the game plays really well. Day and Night cycles are nice. The sun looks great rising. Very animated and pretty.

Seen as this is an Early Access title, I'll start by saying this game has so far baffled me with how much polish it has. Not for an Early Access game. For a game in any stage of development. I expect to have fun in Early Access titles, but I also expect bugs and incompleteness. That is not something that I have seen so far in Portal Knights. Keen Games is serious about this game, and [i]it tells[/i].

I remember when I first started playing Minecraft – past the initial panic of the approaching night (I knew there were zombies) – taking a more detailed look at the game's assets, textures and lighting and thinking to myself "it plays well...", a staple of sandbox games, especially first person, "...but it looks [i]terrible![/i]". After a while, a bit dull as well.

On was my quest to look for the perfect resource pack (then called simply "texture pack") and add-on that would hopefully bring a little more gameplay outside of building massively intricate structures in Creative mode. Finding resource packs that were also compatible with the add-ons I had was a herculean task, but I eventually managed and had a blast while it lasted.

The issue is that, with every update, my texture packs and add-ons would take anything between weeks and months to get updated and I was stuck with playing an older version of the game, fervent to dive into the just-released gameplay.
Portal Knights takes all that anguish and throws it out the window. It delivers, out of the box, not only the smoothest gameplay I've ever seen on a block-sandbox (my 6-year-old system runs this game at 60fps, it's a work of art) but also an alluring, carefully designed graphic style complete with dynamic lighting and custom models for structures, objects and monsters. 

All that is made possible, of course, because of the – admittedly, and quite positively – small bit of lore they've designed the game around. Your world has been shattered by an event called The Fracture and, as such, you will explore small floating islands one by one, by means of [i]*drum roll*[/i] portals! That not only helps gate the content while providing both some peace and an element of progression but also makes the whole game take a smaller toll on your computer. The brief loading screen between the island transition can get annoying, especially if you're moving your home base from one island to another, but in general, it doesn't hinder the gameplay.

Combat is satisfying, if not a little repetitive, at least until you get ahold of some more elaborate spells and skills. My personal opinion is that I am willing to let go of extremely developed combat systems in a game in which I focus on building. It might not be the same for everyone, but then again, if combat is your priority, perhaps you're better off tearing down the latest Diablo III seasonal event.

You can choose to play as either a wizard, warrior or ranger, and they all sell their fantasy reasonably well, each with their specific skill trees that give you access to meaningful choices based on how you prefer playing the game. If that wasn't enough, there are craftable abilities that you can equip with any class, so playing a battlemage, or a druid-like archer isn't completely out of the picture. It might not be [i]optimal[/i], but it will get you through the game just fine. Progressing through the game and seeing all the different enemy and creature models did make me feel like playing another race, but sadly that is not an option in the game's current state. It might come eventually, however, so I'll be patiently waiting. For now, the wide range of character customisation gives me enough tools to tailor a character that resonates with who I am.

More often than not I've been taken aback by how much thought has been given to details and there have been breathtaking moments in which I had to stop and watch a sunset paint the green fields of my home island yellow, and then orange. The sound of birds chirping slowly giving way to the crickets as night falls and the multicoloured sky is filled with stars. Everything looks and sounds solid and lovely – each notch ([i]see what I did there?[/i]) into the stone texture looks right, each hit of your pickax on ore or gem sounds satisfying. It's hard not to want to mine and gather [i]everything[/i] to a point where it feels like your limited bag space and restrictive eight actionbar slots are veritable ball-and-chains.

My only concern considering the state of things has to do with scale, as most of the crafting stations you are able to craft feel like they've been plucked from a giant's house and placed into your house. A drafting table that was supposed to be somewhere you sit on and draw looks like a large physician's whiteboard, the anvil is about the same height as the characters themselves, but the tables and chairs are scaled correctly, so the stark contrast between the stuff that's in your house leaves me wondering what went into their minds when designing these gigantic crafting stations. If they ever implement different races, I wonder what a halfling would feel when entering a standard sized house only to find out he needs a [i]rope[/i] in order to use his workbench.

Finally, some features might be lacking at the moment, such as passive animals, breeding and horseback riding, but those are certain to come, along with many others that will surely feel right when they're introduced.

In general, Portal Knights is an extremely quality title that has already given me multiple hours of fun and it redefines both the sandbox genre and the concept of an Early Access game. It is very close to Minecraft in terms of content (albeit it being [i]different[/i] content) and has room to grow vastly. It plays a lot better too, so if you're looking for an upgrade, Portal Knights is the way to go.

This is one of the few PC games which are split-screen co-op. It's great for kids and non-gamers. This game was the perfect fit for a couch gaming session for me and my wife. We played and beat it and we enjoyed every moment.

If you like Terraria and/or Minecraft, you will most likely love this game. I don't have a lot of time invested, but so far I really like it. 

HOW THE GAME WORKS:
1. You can choose from 3 different classes. Essentially a knight, archer and mage. You gain abilities, weapons and armor sets as you lvl up and progress through each world level.
2. There are 44 worlds to progress through. each have their own theme, enemies and resources. (There are also boss worlds.)
3. The idea is to explore an area, mine its resources then find and repair the portal to the next realm (Sometimes more than one portal.)
4.You can build homes, various workstations, tools, weapons, armor, spells and potions.

The only bad thing I can say, (And this is my opinion.) is that each realm is very small. It takes 15-20min to explore each one. That being said, there are 44 realms and you have to go back to previous realms for specific resources at times, so you get decent use out of most realms. And to be honest it is kind of exciting trying to hurry and get to the next area, because you have no idea what it is!

Also take into account this game is in testing. I personally think this game has a lot of potential.

PROS:
Nice visuals.
Good progression system.
Engaging gameplay.
Really fun co-op play.

CONS:
Some bugs and crashes. (To be expected.)
Small areas.

I like this game a lot and think its worth $15. Try it out!

Graphics: 9/10 Charming and bright in most of the worlds.  I like the graphics alot acutally. They inspire and relax me at the same time and I like that feeling.  With smooth edges, no blockiness, and the game running very smooth with no visible chopping it lends itself to a great gaming experience!

Sound: 6/10 Sound effects are busted! After mining for a few minutes, 20mins or so, the sound effects just stop working! The music is lovely and very peaceful when it should be and exciting/suspenseful when you enter underground caves or mines, almost Metroid like.  Sound would be a 10/10 but with problems of this magnitude...gotta dock 4 points at least.

Gameplay: 9/10 So far the game plays like Minecraft when you are building, and plays like Zelda (any 3d version) when in combat.  The spell/magic system is more than enough to defeat baddies while maintaining proper balance to the Mage's melee counterparts.  The crafting is decent and keeps my interest for hours.  It doesn't take long to craft anything, but you will have to do some grinding and portal hopping to obtain the resources you need.  This isn't like certain mining games where you walk into a cave and 10 types of minerals/metals are there.  This feature kind of forces you to explore the new areas and keeps the game progressing, if you so choose to do so.  I would love it if every world/island had it's own miniboss as this game lost 1 gameplay point for not having enough challenging bosses.  I do like the boss fights but there just aren't enough of them.  Single player, LAN play, and Steam Friends are all options for gameplay so go it alone or with up to 3 other friends! 

Storyline: 7/10 This is pretty basic.  There isn't much of a storyline other than you somehow are a portal knight that is tasked with opening up portals and defending them from the incoming baddies.  There are semi-random NPCs that talk to you, ignore you, or on occassion you will find one that is a trader.  There needs to be more NPCs on each island, a trader for sure!  Other mining sandbox games have villagers in a village...why not add a similar feature to this game so there is a way to get rid of unwanted items instead of just trashing them. In all honesty, this game doesn't need much of a storyline.  It is a sandbox game/Arpg but a strong(er) storyline would definitely help the younger, unfocused, or players that are not as interested in the sandbox aspect. 

Value: 9/10 Even though this game is still in early access and has a few flaws, mainly sound effects quitting out, I would still highly recommend this game to anyone who enjoys a sandbox environment with almost complete freedom to do as you please.  For $15 this is a family friendly game I can stream with my kids and still have fun as an adult.  Portal Knights throws me back to the days of my youth playing console ARPG games. I do wish the game devs would add a 2 or 4 pack in the steam store with a slight discount as this is a coop game and benefits greatly from the multiplayer experience.

Overall score: 8/10 This game is above average in fun, great graphics, super fun multiplayer, family friendly, and runs smoothly on a normal pc/low end gaming rig.  Again I have only 25 hours into this game and have only scratched the surface.  After I have played more I will leave an update and let everyone know if and how things have changed.  Cheers!

Update! This game came out of Early Access and has FIXED all of the above issues that I have pointed out.  The sound is fixed, the multiplayer is fixed AND includes offline split screen for two player coop!  I find that the AI has been improved, graphics have been updated and run smoother than ever, and there are updated textures to items.  I also have noticed that the dev team has balanced the resource requirements of some recipes, added new recipes, added new resources (aka resin), and changed the loot drops for certain monsters. Bomb gazers now drop coal in zones where coal isn't available otherwise, giving you the option to mine coal or hack and slash for it!

Updated score: 9.5/10,  I only ding .5 points because nothing is truly perfect, but this comes really, really close!

This is probably my favorite game of all time. (It's either first, or else second behind Kerbal Space Program). My daughter and I have logged over 500 hours in this game. It's basically Minecraft with a single-player campaign and better graphics, and you can build just about any structure your mind can imagine. We've made castles, cathedrals, modest houses, mansions, and even an entire city where we built a house for every single movable character in the game. There's just so much variety in this game. It's almost impossible to be bored.

I've been playing this game since Early Access, and back then it showed promise. There were plenty of issues, but those are to be expected in an EA game. So I tolerated them, waiting for the developers to work out the bugs and add missing features.
Now, however, that they've gone into full release... I can no longer show any leniency with it. And seeing the positive reception, I feel the need to make my thoughts on the game known.

Behind each game, there is a motivation. A thought that caused it to form. Sometimes it's "I want to make people think", sometimes it's "I want people to get together and have fun", sometimes it's the infinitely less desirable "I want to make money."
For this game... It's pretty obvious that the thought was "I want to make something pretty." The game does look nice. Pretty bland and kind of mobile-y if you ask me, but artstyle is a much more subjective issue. The real problem is that the people behind the game strike me as graphics designers, not game developers. Because while the game looks nice, it is littered with beginner mistakes gameplay-wise. Allow me to list a few.

- The game is an INSANE grindfest. Resources are divided into tiers (portal blocks, ores, gems, etc. all follow this model), like copper to iron to gold as you might be used to if you play any game like this. But here's the catch... Each tier requires more resources. You need more ore to craft a bar, more bars to craft certain items, more portal shards to craft a portal block, and so on. This means that each new tier requires you to spend more time grinding and effectively makes them feel gradually less valuable. You only need to spend a little time gathering copper, but gathering titanium takes forever. And if you play with friends, don't expect to stop whacking those ores with your pickaxe any time soon.

- Random crashing. Sometimes, for no apparent reason (only when playing online as far as I have experienced), your character glitches out entirely after which the game shuts down, sometimes with permanent in-game effects like a loss of money. I remember seeing other varieties of crashing, but that's the only one I distinctly recall. What's worse, sometimes after crashing the game won't even start and you have to reinstall it. This is not acceptable for a "full release".

- Unbalanced classes. The ranger is garbage. Objectively. The mage gets spells, the warrior gets "shouts" that are really just "warrior spells", and the ranger gets... what? In a similar sense, its equipment appears to be worse, it overall underperforms when put next to a warrior or mage, and perhaps worst of all... resin. Because the game wasn't grindy enough. At one point in development, the terrible decision to add resin to the game happened. And now, rangers need to run around chopping down a ton of trees in order to craft most of their equipment. Meanwhile, the equipment of both warriors and mages requires much easier-to-get resources for the most part. Still requires excessive grinding at higher levels though.

- Awful GUI. Look at something like Minecraft. How smooth its inventory management is thanks to a handful of easy-to-use options. Now look at Portal Knights. Its inventory management is terrible. For the longest time there was no way of separating a stack of items, and the best they've done at this point is add a "split stack" option. That's not enough. What if you just want a single item from a stack? You'll have to split it over and over. Why not do it almost exactly like Minecraft? Well, one reason is that right-clicking a stack in this game brings up a menu of options. However I'd argue this menu isn't necessary. It has options like "drop", which already has a special slot for you to put items in. And even if they wanna keep the menu, at least add more useful options. Like the ability to type in the number of items you want to withdraw from the stack. Also, your inventory as well as storages are WAY TOO SMALL for the abundance of items in the game. Prepare to make a ton of chests. And forget where things are constantly.

- A painful lack of variety. The game consists of you moving from island to island, biome to biome, collecting what you need to upgrade your equipment and move on to the next island. However the islands are not distinct enough to make this worth it. The most prevalent reason for this is the enemies. There's only a handful of them, as well as biome-specific varieties. After a handful of islands, you'll barely ever encounter another brand new enemy save for the three bosses. Only cheap reskins with different elements and maaaybe a slightly different attack. And since the game relies so heavily on this exploration, this "journey", this gets monotone very quickly. If there were more side activities, perhaps some that tied into each biome to make them more worthwhile, then this might be more forgivable. As is, the worst part of every new save is having to unlock all the islands. Which is a problem, because it's the main goal of the game.

- Mediocre combat at best. Click a lot. Click nearby if you're a warrior, click far away otherwise. Step to the side when the enemies do their thing, maybe sometimes step backwards or run around a little. That is basically all there is to the combat. Save for the bosses, however they instead all rely on the same tactic. Do a thing, and attack them while they're stunned. For the first and third boss, the thing is to attack something other than the boss. For the second boss, the thing is attacking it in a slightly different yet obvious way that makes it extremely easy.
This level of combat might be acceptable in a game not focused on combat, but well... this one is. And I think the biggest problem isn't what I described here, but the fact that enemies have a huge amount of health, even if your level and equipment is appropriate for the area. The chore of having to wait for each one to die only adds to the grindy feeling of the game. The aforementioned lack of variety also makes it worse, especially in the dungeons which circulate between only a handful of enemies. Of course, another big issue is something that I felt the need to make its own point...

- Plain stupid enemy abilities. This is one of the more evident signs of the developers' lack of understanding of video games. Let's start with blocking. Some enemies have the ability to block. When they do this, they become invulnerable to all attacks. The problem? They randomly do this for several seconds. Which means that once they do it, you just have to stand and wait for them to stop. Blocking should be something very brief, when an attack is expected. The way it's done in this game, it only disrupts the flow of the fight. A more extreme example is the Kupongo enemy (renamed "Alp-Utan" for some inexplicable reason, even though I personally like "Kupongo" way more), which at half health freeze themselves in ice and become invulnerable in the same fashion, for waaay too long. It's a pointless, annoying mechanic that only makes combat even worse.
I think the worst offender however is probably the Fallen Wizard. When these guys die, their resurrect themselves. Not once, not twice, but INDEFINITELY. The only way to permanently kill them is with a weapon that deals Light damage. And here's the thing... There's no in-game indicator that this is the case, and I imagine a lot of players won't bother with Light weapons either because of roleplaying reasons or more likely because there are better alternatives.

I could go on with more examples, I could elaborate on the intolerable lack of swimming in water, other balancing issues, the pointless forced class-specific nature of equipment that prevent multiclassing (which was added in an update, a big mistake like the resin if you ask me), etc. but the character limit is fast approaching... So in summary... This game in no way qualifies for a full release, and I get the impression that the creators have no idea what they're doing.

Portal Knights is a wonderful alternative to the ever popular Minecraft, and much like the aforementioned game, you can dig for resources which are needed to make better and better equipment. Also like Minecraft you can fight mobs of enemies for crafting items and XP and here is where Portal Knights differs, XP levels actually improve your abilities, allowing you to fight stronger foes of course you're going to want to upgrade your equipment before taking them on.

Another difference is you can upgrade your crafting stations using different materials and there are different side quests and events to participate in.

All in all Portal Knights is a fun, relaxing experience for people of all ages and I can't recommend this game enough.

Great game! Imagine Terraria, Minecraft, Animal Crossing, Zelda with a little Dark Souls (My opinion) and you have Portal Knights! Great art style, amazing sound design with some of the best music ive heard in a game in awhile (sounds kinda like harry potter score meets tim burton). Combat mechanics are basic zelda type combat, Attack and dodge. Tons of crafting in the game with armor sets that vary and look amazing.

If you are a fan of any of the games ive listed above then i urge you to buy this game now while its 11.99!

This is not Minecraft. Beyond the aesthetic, this is a completely different game. Ultimately, for an early acces game, this is great, especially for a younger market that are showing interest in RPG style games. There is room for improvement, but on a whole it feels like more than you normally get from early access with a lot of meat on the bones and I'm looking forward to seeing the updates. For 15 bucks, get around it.

Obviously targetted at a younger market, the combat is a little reptitive and the only real objective is to upgrade your gear through a crafting system which is admittedly quite deep, but the pacing of the game is a little slow. There are a number of different armours and weapons that you can craft and use, regardless of your class, which is great, but farming the materials for these items can be quite laborious, bordering on tedious.

The RPG elements aren't that deep. Character progression is rather linear, with only minor choices at certain levels with a "this or that" perk choice. The creative side of the game seems irrelevant to me, comparing to Minecraft, I see no reason to really put time into building a base in this game as you're jumping worlds so often that you'd never have time to appreciate your work. Chuck the tables and workbenches down, and that's all you'll need.

The combat is very - spam click, dodge roll, spam click - at least for the mage. The dodge mechanic can be very clunky, and the TAB targetting is absolute trash. That being said, there's still something rewarding about going around kicking enemy heads in. The enemy models are really nice, everything in this game is lovely to look at. When the dodge mechanics work properly, the combat isn't very challenging. They encourage you to play with friends, but I honestly can't really see how local multiplayer would work outside of boss battles.

This is a jewel of a game. I play it with my two young children. They love it, it is cartoony, lovely, bricks are fun and diverse enough for casual play with kids. We build castles, underground bunkers, have fun with lovely monsters, who never die, you just send them away when you overcome them. Monsters are not scary, even the bosses are lovely. 

Character progression and item creation is just right for this sort of play. And it is not nearly that addictive as World Of Warcraft for example, which means it’s OK to introduce it to the kids. We have this game now for like 2 years and play it from time to time. I managed to end it with a breeze and that alone it was worth the money. Fun with kids tripled or quadrupled its value, although I bought 3 versions – one for myself and two for my kids.

All in all, I highly recommend this game to anyone who would like to play a computer game with his or her kids. Or even if you feel young at heart and don’t want to struggle with character development and game mechanics and just want some fun and action and feeling of progression. If that is your thing, than this game will deliver!

I've played a stupid amount of this game for an early access title.  This may not be a comprehensive guide, but it's long enough that I feel like it will give people a realistic glimpse into what to expect. 

Things that rock about this game:

*  Large universe is LARGE.  The home island that I have customized the most seems small at first Glance.  I've been carving out huge swaths to make new buildings, dungeons, gardens, and landscaping projects as time goes on, yet an aeriel view on the smallest looking Island reveals I've still barely scratched the surface - and that's saying nothing about the vast caverns beneath.

*  Events.  There are some fun and interesting events.  The great part is resources.  Some of the rarest Items in the game come from these events, and certainly the most interesting monsters.

*  Soundtrack.  It's not my first choice in music style.  The compositions are solid throughout, and the clarity is top notch.  There is no 8-bit feel here - the instruments could (and might be, for all I know) real.  

*  Pets.  The basic pets can be cool.  The rare pets are fantastic!  There is something satisfying about having a baby boss follow me around.  Cats, mice, owls, a panda, dragons (though I've only seen one), and a mini end boss adds a certain flair I find pleasing.

*  Blocks.  I've never played minecraft so perhaps I am not the best choice to comment on this, but there are some beautiful and interesting blocks in this game.  Carpets, intricate carved hard stones, shiny gem blocks, several shades of concrete, and various stone and wood blocks are sweet.  The _real_ cool ones are the neon and meteorite blocks.  Some are lit but cast no light, others are so bright a few too many in a room is blinding.

*  Co-op.  You can solo online or off, but the real fun when it comes to combat is with friends.  Multiplayer combat is fun to play around with, and effective.

*  Graphics. it's cartoonish, but it's all smooth and polished looking.  Curves aren't much of a reality in a box-block game, but none of the graphics are pixelated or jagged.  Edges are sharp.  Colors are vivid.

*  Lighting options.  Braziers, torches, chinese lanterns, candycane striped fixtures, colored lamps, Star lanterns, chandelier style fixtures, and some blocks make for some fun and interesting lighting patterns.

*  Statues.  Knights, gargoyles, lions, dragons, golden eggs, toads and giant alligator demigods give the option of some truly unique decoration styles.

*  Planting and gardening.  Putting aside the counterpoint to this I'm putting below, it's sweet to not have to judge lighting conditions, water, soil types, or much of anything - plant a seed and it grows!  Underwater gardens and floating forests are possible and beautiful once finished.  

*  Character models.  So many options!  Better yet, they aren't restrictive in the least.  Just to test I put together a female character with a vibrant green pixie cut, bone ear necklace, monster eyes and a goatee.  It may not be a huge sell to many, but I ADORE the ability to customize any character as I like with all options in the game.  This is one of the few that truly does.

*  Vanity Items - Care for a monocle to go with your bumblebee wings and fluffy bunny pants?  Perhaps some jester/harlequin pants and shoes to Liven up your formal Mandarin robes?  Some Devil horns to make sure your enemies know you mean no good?  There are **way** more items than are displayed in the wiki page.  The best part is you don't have to give up armor bonuses!  Wear your armor and look like a million bucks at the same time! 


Things that are not so awesome:

*  No access to water blocks.  You can craft water bombs to make pools, but the option for a player to use an item capable of creating such beauty is currently stripped from the game.  There is still fountains that generate with a world, but you can't collect them.  The water is **gorgeous**, and it's a shame that by and large we'll only ever see it during an event or in an underground cavern.

*  Enemies.  Each biome has it's own variants, but it feels like the same 10 monsters everywhere I go.  There are more than 10; but most of it is variations on slimes, skeletons, mummies, wraiths, turtles, and ogres.  There are a couple of really neat ones, like the merman and dogfish, that are truly rare.  For the most part once you've made it about 1/3 of the way through the game you've about seen them all outside of an event.

*  Event generation.  There are some creative and fun events that pop up, but whether by design or by accident it's been common for me to get the same event several days in a row.  There are some super cool trophies to get out of this but I'm about full on mummy and Bones trophies.

*  Combat mechanics.  I enjoy not having to read a tactics manual to do the combat.  The warrior is solid.  While the ranger and the mage are different, the execution of the attacks feels so similar t

*  Pet AI.  I know this is petty, but some of the coolest pets have a frustrating habit of blocking part of your view during combat in first person.  Doubly frustrating when it intereferes with building or causes you to walk off of an edge because it won't move away from a hole.

*  Difficulty scale.  It's a challenge at first.  To be fair, there is a balance through most of the game.  Once I got around level 27 that slipped, and once I hit 30 my choices were no challenge at all or a hard mode boss.  C'thiris kind of makes up for it, but one level isn't quite enough to recover from that.

*  biome restrictions on planting.  There are all sorts of cool flowers, trees, fruits and vegetables in this game.  A genuine plethora of colorst, shapes and textures.  I see all of these and imagine the gorgeous landscapes I could put together.  instead I plant a forest with perhaps three trees, two bushes, and and a couple veg.  I know it may not be the point of the game.  It is the part I most enjoy and a huge focus, however, so I don't feel like this is an unimportant complaint.

*  The lack of an ending.  This may end up being an obsolete complaint come release day.  At the moment you fight the end(?) boss, go to a portal at the end of the world, Aaaaaaand nothing.  No credits.  No congratulations.  Just a portal that doesn't activate or lead anywhere.  I suspect that part of the full release or an upcoming DLC will use this.  For the moment it is little more than a decoration and ambiguous sign of victory that isn't particularly satisfying.

*  Disappearing data.  I haven't had this happen in a few weeks, but I have lost three characters and two universes to...gremlins?  Elves?  I'll never know.  The error message that pops up and reads "data error" is accurate but uninformative.  It also was almost enough to ruin the game completely for me.  It did for a bit.  I now back up my files after every session, which is useful but leaves me with a kind of distrustful feeling.

The TL;DR
It has some flaws and frustrations.  The enjoyment of the pros far outweigh the cons, however, and if you like building, exploring, crafting, and having fun solo or with friends there are scores of hours of enjoyment to be found here.

This game hasn't just been fun for me as an old gamer, whose first console was Mattel’s Intellivision, Portal Knights has been a fun time for me to spend with my daughter.
It gives us both the chance to explore creativity where the only limit is imagination. Her buildings have been very original for a 10 year old mind. By building together, we are building towns and small kingdoms together. 
Its not a perfect game but this is one of our go-to games when it comes to the age old answer to the statement ‘I’m bored!’

I found this game when I a kid and I still play now. I am not the biggest gamer, but if I want something more cozy, this game is at the top of my list. The music is one of my favourite parts of the game.

Portal Knights is a pretty fun game, similar to minecraft but with some RPG elements. The issue is that the game is very simple and leaves you with the same formula throughout which is a monototonous game of traveling to find upgrade materials to upgrade your gear and learn skills.

Another issue is there are only 7 hotbar spaces for tools, your weapon AND spells. It leaves you with few options if you want to go out and adventure with torches and pickaxe in hand since you'll need at least 3/4ths of your bar for combat. 

The class system in this game is nice with decent customization but although the game gives you many options most of them are just objectively bad.

While I had fun playing Portal Knights and will likely keep playing it when I'm really bored I can't reccomend anyone else really do so, the game can be frustrating in it's tedium and lackluster in many ways.

Oh and in multiplayer when you teleport to another world which you'll have to OFTEN due to each world having different resources...all your friends get teleported too. This game is not multiplayer friendly and trying to work together to organize where the team will go to get what each class needs is a painful dilemma.

Get it on sale for half price.

Gonna get into the meat of this right away: If you are planning on buying this to play with your friends - don't. The multiplayer system this game uses is very bad. Any time anyone in your game wants to move to another island to gather materials for crafting - YOUR ENTIRE party has to come too. You can't set up a base and build because your entire party has to leave the island when someone needs to make a run to get building supplies. Does someone need to travel to another island quickly to get a few gems to make something? EVERYONE COMES WITH YOU. There isn't even any affirmation or anything... every single player is suddenly forced into a loading screen if anyone in the server initiates a load.

Portal Knights is totally awesome, especially for families that love to game together. I've been wishing for a casual game like this for years and finally found it. I am extremely happy with the game.

First, some background. 4-player co-op is the sweet spot for us.  We (myself, my wife and our two daughters, 18 and 9) are always on the hunt for high-quality co-op games, which are sadly hard to find. I think it is safe to say we rank as insane boardgame and RPG addicts. We have over the years all played and loved games like World of Warcraft, Minecraft, Torchlight II, the Diablo series and The Elder Scrolls series (not the MMO). Yes, I know Skyrim is not a co-op game, but I mention it here because it is so compelling with Nexusmods that we play it both alone and together with friends despite the lack of co-op.

With roughly 75 hours into Portal Knights so far, we are still hooked and I think we are only midway through the game. In my opinion, this game is a vast improvement over Minecraft, which never held my attention for long even though my kids got hooked on it. 

We really enjoy some of Portal Knights' limited-time events and we especially enjoyed the recent 2017 Christmas adventure event. During the holiday break, my youngest kept pestering us to play the game every chance she got. We all enjoyed it together, but she was the driving force to get us to play Portal Knights over our other options (mainly boardgames).

I was totally blown away by how fun it is to literally loot the dungeon, which is an experience I have not seen in any other game. What I mean is that the random loot drops you get are insignificant compared to the joy of actually chiseling a sweet statue off the wall and then deciding to also take the wallstones, flooring, doors, gates, carpets and lamps as well because they will look amazing in the new wing of your ever-expanding homemade clan castle or village. Before we'd even finished exploring a dungeon, we would already be literally tearing the place apart!

Honestly, this aspect to the game is so brilliant, unexpected, and unique that it deserves a major industry award. Imagine if Fallout 4 let you harvest parts directly from an enemy camp or vault so you could haul it back to your own settlement.

With all that said, here are some thoughts on the pros and cons of this game:

Pro:
- Fantastically addictive mix of co-op sandbox world building and MMO-style crafting.
- Brings an amazing new dynamic to looting not found in other games: literally loot the whole dungeon itself.
- Just enough RPG elements to give each class it's own style (wizard, archer, and knight).
- Exploration, resource mining and looting both familiar and unique enough to surprise you.
- Combat is simple enough that younger players don't feel useless.
- Excellent controller support.
- Great graphics supporting a wide range of GPUs.
- Works well on Windows 10.

Con: 
- Probably not as much fun to play by yourself. Having a team is critical in some areas, especially during events. Showing a friend what you just built is half the fun.
- Simple combat system will not hold your attention for long if you are used to more complex combat.
- Level progression and RPG elements are extremely simplistic.
- If you don't like casual sandbox games, this is not going to keep you interested for very long.
- The storyline is so completely forgettable that it barely even exists, which is strange for a game with so many RPG-like elements.

To start, I normally don't play primarily single player games.

NOTE: The game is advertised as 'multiplayer', however you do need Steam friends (Which I don't have any :( ) to play Multiplayer, OR you can play on LAN.

Pros:

-Visually Stunning
The bloom effect is a very nice touch, I love the character modeling, I like the variety of gear.

-Tutorial
The tutorial is laid out very simply, and if you could imagine the controls of your standard MMORPG smacked with Minecraft, Portal Knights is the result (NOT hard to understand at all!)

-Character and Game Progression
This is both a Pro and a Con, I'll touch more on the Con of this later; I enjoy the simplicity of the overall character building and also how clear the objective is.

-Dainty Maps
By this I mean the maps do have a lot to explore, however they are just perfectly sized to where you can explore each individual map in a timely fashion while also taking in the visuals around you.

-Variety
Each area you are faced with has really stunning visuals with themed blocks that fit that specific biome. Unlike Minecraft (I use Minecraft because it's something we can all relate to), where you can leave one biome and enter another, in Portal Knights, you take a portal and enter a new island with a biome/theme.

-Combat
HONESTLY, going into this I thought I'd hate the combat, yes it does involve a lot of clicking, however each monster has its own little special ability (Yes, sometimes they hurt, a lot) and you can dodge/roll with your character in attempt to avoid their attacks; after awhile it gets really fun to engage a few monsters at once.

-STUNNING VISUALS
I really have to say it again, this game IS FREAKING BEAUTIFUL, and honestly it doesn't lagg, at all, the framerate is GREAT, and the game looks ohh so divine, I just want to eat the berries right off of the bushes.

The building system is great, there's a huge variety of blocks offered to build with and you can really design your house how you want, and you can even set an island as your home and get back to it any time (And use it as a base of operations). I look forward to building more in the future, and I hope they add more ores/block types.

-Villages/Doodads
This really goes hand in hand with the visuals, but there's little dungeons scattered around above and underground that you can go into and get loot or find rare ores/items, you can also harvest blocks to add to your house.

-Crafting
The crafting system is actually pretty straightforward, it's really simple to discard items, and the material requirements are laid out really easily, and crafting an item is as simple as the click of a button, it's also really visually appealing as well.

These are a few things of many that this game will offer you, I highly recommend it and it's completely worth your dime, as well as your time.


Cons:

Honestly I'm really grasping for straws here to think of anything really negative that I would have to say. It's HARD with this game, I really have thoroughly enjoyed my time playing it.

-Character/Game Progression
As stated above in the Pros segment, I'd touch on the Cons a little down here. My only (Very small) complaint is that the gameplay can get a tad repetative and grindy, however I stand by the fact that the game enables you to create your own adventure, and there's plenty to do, so it really isn't too bad.

Portal Knights is a digging adventure game in the same vein as Terraria or Minecraft. 

[h1]Basic Gameplay Loop [/h1]
Mostly you will be hopping from portal to portal, leveling up, crafting new weapons and armor, and...well getting to the next portal. (also building things if you so desire). The game isn't an infinite world like Minecraft. Rather it's a bunch of randomly generated bite sized worlds strung together with portals. When you enter a new world...island.....shattered land...place, you'll have to explore and find the portal gate. The gate starts off empty though, so you'll have to fill it with "portal stones." You get these stones by doing basically anything. Killing enemies, mining things, and finishing dungeons will sometimes land you some portal stone fragments. When you fill the portal with said stones, it opens up to another island. The islands are really small. I've only had one that had any kind of underground network. I think they could do with being a bit bigger.

[h1]Atomphere and Aesthetic[/h1]
The game has a very light hearted adventure atmosphere with a "cute" aesthetic. This is no voxel game though. The only thing that's square is the ground (and structures). I feel the ground has enough little details like grass and rocks to make it not stick out like a sore thumb. Worlds range from the usually foresty plains and deserts to toxic mushroom lands and tundras. The biomes are all filled with appropriate enemies and vegetation. The lighting is very nicely done, giving things a warm look in light. Overall it looks pretty nice. Dungeons can be a bit samie though.

[h1]Combat[/h1]
This is a huge part of the game, so I'm going to split it down further.

[b]General Combat[/b]
While looking for portal gates, you will be fighting whatever monsters are on the world. Combat is very zelda-esque. When you hit an enemy, the camera locks on automatically. While locked on, the jump button turns into a roll button, which is kind of a pain. What if I want to jump in a fight? Well too bad. You can't fight with the camera unlocked either. You CAN unlock the camera, but as soon as you hit something again it will re-lock. Sometimes the camera will lock onto the wrong enemy if you start by using a ranged attack.

[b]Combat Problems[/b]
THIS GAME IS TOO EASY. That's the biggest problem with the game. 
Most of the fighting so far is just holding the mouse button until things die, with the ocassional roll. If you have a ranged weapon then its all over, you've won. Melee enemies can't jump or find a way up a 2 block height, so you're free to wail on them until they die. Even if you're on even ground, they slowly walk at you while taking hits. Your melee hits push foes backwards, so sometimes you accidentally hit them out of range. This can be annoying if the knockback lets them get another hit in on you.

[b]Enemy Types - What Do You fight?[/b]
[list]
[*]Basic melee enemies that run up and hit you. Sometimes they have unique attacks like turtlemen popping inside their shell and spinning at you like Gamera(or Bowser).
[*]Spellcasting Enemies that will launch their spell.......and then run up and try to hit you, until their spell recharges. Spells include AoE spots on the ground that do damage or basic elemental projectile attacks.
[*]Unique enemies/MiniBosses that usually run up and try to hit you. sometimes they have special elemental effects on their hits. 
[*]Annoying Flying enemies that ram you from the sky. So basically they run up and hit you.
[*]Flying Eyeballs that have unavoidable attacks. no matter when you dodge, they WILL hit you. Screw those things. Run up and hit them....but with ranged. Good luck hitting them with melee.
[*]Big Bosses that have their own stage an mechanics. The one that I fought was a pretty fun time.
[/list]
[b]Combat Stlyes - How Do You Fight[/b]
At the start of the game you can pick between 3 classes. Warrior, Ranger, Mage.
These classes only change the passive spells you get when reaching certain levels. The only semi interesting one is at level 30. Every class can use every weapon, there are no stat requirements for weapons. There are basically 3 ways to make things' hp bar go to zero. Melee Weapons, Ranged Weapons, and Spells. 
[u]Melee Weapons[/u] are everything from Swords, Clubs, Axes, etc. Good luck hitting flying things with melee.
[u]Ranged Weapons[/u] are Bows, Crossbows, Slingshots, Magic Wands, ect.
[u]Spells[/u].....well in the first tier of the game's crafting the only offensive spell you can get is a Lightning Bolt. The other 2 spells you can get are a healing spell, and a battlecry damage buff spell. Spells have mana costs and cooldowns.

Your Armor also plays a part in your damage dealing, giving you passive bonuses such as critical hit chance or bonus melee damage.

[b]Phat Lootz[/b]
 Killing all this stuff must give some good loot right? Special Armor, Rings, or Weapons.
 NOPE. Killing things gives you crafting materials and XP. Speaking of Crafting Materials...

[h1]Crafting[/h1]
Crafting is the other big part of the game. You mine ore, kill things, and then make items from it. Craft armor, weapons, spells (yes you have to craft those), and decorations. The only problem I have with crafting is that sometimes you never find some of the things you need. I needed something for a spell that I just never got any of. This could be due to the random nature of the game, but when the one offensive spell that I can use sucks and I can't find the materials to upgrade it, I'm gonna throw off the wizard hat and go run up and hit things. When an item finishes crafting (sometimes it takes a few seconds to craft, sucks if you need to make a lot of that thing) It just sits in the crafting statioin. You have to manually click the finished item for it to go into your inventory. 

[h1]Building Things?[/h1]
You can change the land block by block to get it how you want, there's a few decorations and a lot of different plant life to decorate gardens with. Didn't mess with this much, but it's there....

[h1]Closing Thoughts[/h1]
The game is pretty good right now. Here's a quick Pro and Con list because those are fun.
Pros
[list]
[*] Game looks good
[*] Lots of Weapons and Armor to Choose From
[*] Sense of Adventure is Pretty Good
[*] Boss Was fun
[*] Different Envirnments and Enemies
[/list]
Cons
[list]
[*] Early game Spell Options Very Limited....and by limited I mean they kinda suck
[*] Individual Worlds Are Very Small
[*] Combat Problems. Mainly the Lock On
[*] TOO EASY!
[/list]

I feel like most of these Cons can be fixed though. The foundation for the game seems pretty solid. I look forward to how it will develop. Hopefully it WILL develop.

This game can't decide whether it wants to be a survival crafting game or an adventure rpg game, and ends up doing neither well. Base building and setting up crafting stations directly conflicts with the games theme of continuously moving through tiny sandbox levels killing baddies. There's no reason to explore much since every cave is barren of anything, save for the occasional dungeon with the same 2 enemies for each one, so you're left with just hunting for the portal to the next level as soon as you get the few needed materials found on the surface. Ultimately ends up a polished but shallow experience.

The game is pretty much fun. Much more so with friends, but it's a good timesink; you can always find a thing to work toward or accomplish, the combat is fairly simple but arcade-y, and the little patterns/layouts of the places you explore are sort of fun. It's very repetitive, especially noticeable when the same underground room appears multiple times in a row in the same area. A lot of the content is very samey but again, the fact you can shift focus if you're bored of a particular part of the game helps alleviate it.

The reason I can't recommend it is that it has now crashed for me multiple times in a way that will softlock you out of large parts of the game. Essentially, if it crashes during loading/gets stuck on a black screen then (despite very long load and regular "save" icon flashes) it will usually roll back your inventory a fair bit back but keep the world mostly saved. So, if you lose an item required to unlock a boss, or a fairly rare reward, or a quest item that cannot be replaced such an as NPC, you are out of luck. Not to mention that recipes for items are considered items too. Considering the time-sinky nature of the game, the fact that loading times are for some reason horrific, and that crashes can then undo time spent *or worse, prevent progress on a save*, I just can't recommend anyone pick it up.

By the way, it can get stuck when you select quit game from the main menu. So even if you go back to the main menu, log out of a character, then hit exit, it will still delete *some but not all* save file progress, which is a bit of a slap in the face. At least for me, there is no way to stop playing the game without risking losing progress.

It's fun enough, but it's just not worth the caveats above for me. It's a shame because I did generally enjoy spending time, doubley so with friends, but it's just not worth the sinking feeling of losing hours of time because you didn't leave an item in a storage box before going to a different area, and the game decided to load for a few moments and then get "stuck". Probably not going to come back, if only because of the sour taste it left me after losing a 4 hour play session of progress for the second time.

It has all the elements necessary for a fantastic game. Good music, great building, good art style, good exploration, good crafting, decent biomes, decent controls, and treasure. But...

[b]Music:[/b] 
It's quite immersive and enjoyable, but sometimes it double-starts and plays the same track over itself. Very annoying and five years after release, unacceptable.

[b]Building:[/b]
This part seems to stand out to me. While it's just block-by-block building, there are a lot of varieties of blocks and objects that can be crafted/found. Physics don't really come into play, so you can build whatever you want in whatever shape you want. This is what I've found to be the most enjoyable part of the game so far.

[b]Art style:[/b] 
Great, although a bit more variety between mobs, treasure chests, dungeons, and pre-made structures would have helped.

[b]Exploration:[/b] 
So far, pretty good, but my biggest gripe is that some dungeons have VERY little worth finding, and some have absolutely nothing at all. Don't make me fight mobs and jump around through the darkness with no pay off. 

[b]Crafting:[/b] 
Frankly, the crafting is fine. Good progression, materials are pretty accessible, and the items you create feel (and are) stronger than what you had before. My only problem is with the item-crafting timer, which seems fairly pointless in a single player/co-op experience with no PvP.

[b]Biomes:[/b] 
They vary to certain degrees, but eventually they all seem to blend together a bit. This is partly to do with mobs and pre-built structures crossing biome boundaries. When I see the same creatures and buildings in varying landscapes, those landscapes start to feel the same.

[b]Controls:[/b]
The controls are pretty good. If you hate that it switches you from first-person to third during combat, there's an option in the settings that will fix that.

[b]Treasure:[/b]
The treasure boxes mostly look the same, which is acceptable, but a lot of them have simple materials in them, such as iron or palm leaves. I didn't just spend fifteen minutes chopping through skeletons and flying eyeballs to get something I could have mined on the surface. A few chests have had armour and weapons in them, but not enough.

[b]TL;DR:[/b]
A good game with a lot of varying blocks and objects with which to craft your house/workshop. Biomes are pretty good to explore, but it will feel like a bit of a grind after a while. Buy it if you like crafting, exploring and building, but wait for a sale and don't expect to dump in hundreds of hours.
