If you like mining for materials, building structures, fighting mobs and falling off islands placed precariously in the sky then Portal Knights might be the game for you.

Character creation gives you a choice of 3 classes: Fighter, Mage or Archer and is pretty minimal. It's interface feels like you're creating a Nintendo Mii rather than creating anything complex and the characters have a rounded Lego look to them. Each class has abilities that they learn as they level up although some choices are somewhat confusing: the warrior uses STR as his primary stat so at level 15 he can increase his agility or int which are both pointless for him. The archer can increase STR (melee damage) or Int - again, both pointless?

Once you've created your character you're dropped on the starter world and given a series of quests to handhold you through the learning process of how things work. Once those have been completed the quests vanish and you're on your own from there to do what you want.

Once on an island defeating monsters (and, to a lesser degree, mining) gives you portal shards and these are used in the creation of portal stones via the crafting system and six of these special stones placed in one of the defunct portals around the island will power it up and permanently re-enable it for use. This gives you your gateway to another island and is Portal Knights method of progression. 

There are 4 types of Portal stone that you can create and each colour stone takes a differing number of shards - the early starter worlds are accessed using blue portals and blue portal stones only take two blue shards to create each stone. Yellow portals start to appear around level 10 and yellow portal stones take 3 yellow shards so higher level portal stones take more materials to make. A portal will need 6 stones to activate it.

Travelling to another island opens up new blocks, ores, plants and mobs and each island can have multiple portals dotted around it. There's usually a dungeon too and these start off quite small but grow to a decent size on the later levels and are wonderfully lit. Mob variation within the dungeons seems a bit restricted though as far as I've seen - there's flying eyeballs, skeletons and..well, thats about it really.

Once you get to a certain point progression-wise you'll find one of the portals will take you to a special island. This only has a single mob on it and is a good, old fashioned boss fight. No spoilers here but its an interesting mechanic to drop in between the island exploring and isnt just a straight forward hold-fire-until-its-dead fight.

Crafting could probably do with a mention too. It reminds me somewhat of Starbounds crafting system in that you need specific machines to make different bits and those bits are used in other machines to make items (ie use a furnace to smelt ore > bars then use the workbench to fashion the bars into weapons).

When you craft something though it stays in the machine until you click it rather than going directly into your inventory. This is somewhat annoying but Im guessing this is so you can set up large batches of things that take a while and then go do something else while its crafting.

Overall its a very pretty game thats quite polished considering its just come into early access but obviously it still has its bugs. Quite a few people have had crashes/startup errors although the only ones I've personally seen have been a placement graphic bug (it was showing a doorway instead of the correct graphic when trying to place a chest) and a crash to desktop when I used a grenade to blow up a wall because I was too idle to mine it manually.

Tips:
-  Press M to get the map up. On the map screen clicking on a world will let you set that world as your home world or travel to it allowing quick travel to any world you've opened up. Clicking the tabs at the top of that screen will show you what mobs, plants and ores that world has. Useful if you're looking for something specific.
- On the map screen pressing the icon at the bottom right will port you to the entrance zone in point. Useful if you're stuck down a mine/on a cliffside and cant get back to the surface. Clicking the icon on the bottom left ports you to your home world (home world can be set from the map screen too).
- Things like doors/windows/furniture/statues in dungeons can be destroyed and picked up for use in your home. I found it particularly useful to rob the nearest dungeon of its doors to keep the drafts out of my new house.
- The level of the crafting machines define the number of recipes it has access to. Get the materials and upgrade them (up arrow icon at the far right of its interface) to get access to new, higher level stuff.
- Armour isnt class dependant. Any class can equip any armour/use any weapon.
- If you're a Warrior and having problems with flying things, carry a bow around as well as your main weapon.

Pros
+ Graphics engine is very pretty especially its lighting.
+ Music is also very good.
+ Crafting is in, working and already quite evolved.
+ Boss fights!
+ Leveling up and selectable skills for your character.

Cons
- Islands are miniscule and need to be considerably larger. This is my one major gripe about this game - there's hardly any exploration as you can pretty much see from one side of the zone to the other and cross it in about 60 seconds.
- Islands are also somewhat samey. So far I've seen 1 desert biome, 1 snow biome, 1 swamp biome and 11 green/leafy biomes. Hoping that gets a bit more varied in the terms of ratios of different types.
- The combat lock-on is annoying. I *know* I can hit tab to retarget. I dont need to be told every single fight.
- Cant rebind any of the keys.
- No real graphics options other than resolution,Window/Fullscreen and AA. There's also a Screen border x/y slider but I couldnt see that do anything?
- No run button. It feels odd to get attacked by something and then just nonchalantly wander away from it.

TLDR;
Very pretty game in the Cubeworld/Trove/Minecraft family. A few aspects of it are still buggy but overall its quite slick. Worth picking up if you're into those types of games (especially with the 20% off this week).

Its buggy (which is to be expected in an early access title) but its building a solid foundation for a great game.

Now that I hear that there is potentially a Portal Knights 2 on the way next year, I figured I wanted to write a review knowing that the chances of any of the problems this game have being fixed are slim to none.

Portal Knights is Minecraft if it focused more on RPG than building. You can still make a nice house or giant golden dildo but with less options if you wanted it to be something other than golden. But on the flipside the level system is nice for seeing progress with your character, with some weapons and armour being locked behind level requirements. Even when playing solo for the main story it's well worth a try.

Now for the thing that really pissed me off:

No scaling in difficulty for additional players: Playing solo is great right up until the optional harmode versions of the bosses. For a game that never really expects you to have to grab a friend to complete anything it suddenly turns around and says "Fuck you ya lonesome chode" and locks the best loot behind impossible bosses (unless you're an avid Soulsborne speedrunner). Alternatively if you turn up with 3-4 people to these bosses then you've won, no matter what class or equipment you've got. Even if a character dies it's a short trip back to the boss where you can drop in and fight as normal, with the bosses resetting only when all players are out of the arena. The worst part? Not even guaranteed drops, which means if you're struggling with 2 players to beat a boss and they don't drop what you're after then screw you fight it again.

TLDR: Great for RPG Minecraft, shit for single player in post game.

Portal Knights bids a fond wink and a nod to what I would assume was a large inspiration - Minecraft; and I'm a big fan of both!  On the surface this game may seem like a cheap clone, but it actually takes the gameplay in a much different direction, which in my opinion is its biggest strength (it also adds a ton of small quality-of-life elements that make some things so much easier).  It maintains the accessibility and creative aspects of the sandbox genre, but the RPG elements laid over top feel really natural and compliment the gameplay.  Building is fun and rewarding, as the natural landscapes and fairly full palette of materials can make some really good-looking structures.  Combat is nicely varied and, while maybe a bit simplistic, is adaptable enough that different classes feel like different personalities and styles - which adds to the replay-ability too!  Speaking of, if you find yourself enjoying the game then you'll easily lose days of free time as you work through item and character progression, try different builds, explore countless randomly-generated dungeons and events, and try to find every last hidden chest, craft, and- oops, it's 1am.  And it's three days later.  And I'm still on my first playthrough.

Overall, this game is a very charming and very relaxing way to spend a good amount of time, and while it has some fairly minor flaws that are easily overshadowed by how much it has going for it, I genuinely felt like this game was well worth the money and time.

Portal Knights, at first glance, looks like a pretty remake of Minecraft. It has the same blocky, cartoony charm, and does have exploring, fighting, mining and building as its main features. The game is, in some ways remarkably similar, but in other ways, remarkably different.

I'll be using spoiler tags to hide both challenge-reducing tactics as well as actual game spoilers (for those who want to experience the game with zero advance knowledge, which can actualy provide a lot more fun to the game for first playthrough).

[h1]Class/Leveling system[/h1]
The class and leveling systems offer some options for how you'd like to experience the game.  Warrior focuses on melee damage, Ranger focuses on bows and evasion tactics, and Mage focuses on spells and elemental weaknesses. All classes (as of this post) can use all armors, have a mana bar, and can use all skills, though due to primary stat gains on levelup, all classes will perform their niche better than the others, as expected. That said, you can totally hand a warrior a magic staff or a ranger a battleaxe and theyll use it no problem.

Combat in general is loads of fun and, when you're progressing normally, a decent challenge. The dodging mechanic brings some fun to it, and the game will punish you pretty harshly for not avoiding damage, which in some regards is really refreshing. I got some Ocarina of Time flashbacks with the dodging and lockon systems, doding and then striking my foe, then blindsided by another random foe that just showed up, or dodging across the landscape because it's far faster than any movement speed bonus ever is. Most enemies have some kind of ranged magic attack[spoiler], and the majority of boss damage is magic, which puts mage's magic resist talent as one of the best survivability options in the game. Combined with a high base mana total, the healing spell, and the ability to equip tons of HP bonuses, it makes mage surprisingly the most durable class in the game, which, while i enjoy mages myself, feels pretty backwards[/spoiler].

Magic follows an "opposing elements" theme [spoiler] which is further reinforced by hardmode bosses[/spoiler], fire and ice are weak to each other, electro and nature are weak to each other, and light(holy) and dark(astral) are weak to each other. Mage needs to focus on exploiting these weaknesses. At endgame stats, the difference in damage between the early nature staff and the later game [spoiler]holy[/spoiler] staff is not much after weakness bonus is applied, so [b]none of the elements are strictly better than the others[/b] simply due to weapon power rating, which is a very nice thing to see. The spells, while only one spell (with varying ranks) exists per element, have specific uses, and are good in some despite the enemy you face.

Levelups yield some customizable stat points as well as a few instant primary stat allocations. You gain talents at specific levels (2, 5, and then every 5th) and they all lend something to the class or something generally useful to the game (except that level 10 talent for all classes [spoiler] 10% bonus exp, useless at cap[/spoiler] ). All talents can be hot-swapped without having to be anyplace specicif or spending something. You can open the menu and change your build whenever you like, but you only get one talent per tier, but there's no pressure to really specialize your talent build. There is an item in game that will allow you to reset your stat allocations, so if you screw up, you can redo it.

[h1]Worlds, Characters, and Equipment[/h1]
The islands are undeniably beautiful and fun. Each Island has a biome, and its own list of spawns, plants, and resources, and are plainly shown to the player on selection from the world map. It's easy to know where to go for a specific resource or enemy, and that is glorious. It definately aids in the building and equipment progression aspects of the game, and is a very welcome feature. The game is further enhanced by the ability to simply "step" up one full block without jumping.

One thing about PKs that im conflicted on is the separation of Worlds and Characters. On one hand, it's nice to take my fully leveled character to a new world [spoiler]with all the portal stones needed to progress straight to the end of the game[/spoiler] and just have fun tearing through it or mine more resources that my already mined world lacks, and on the other hand, the first time I brought a new character to a completed world with full [spoiler]titanium-level[/spoiler] gear and went straight to the final areas and leveled to 30 in under an hour. I feel this really diminishes the replay value of the adventure since many players will want to get to level cap ASAP. While the game offers you the choice, I fear most players will take that choice, which really reduces the adventuring lifespan of the game.

[h1]Building[/h1]
Building takes a lot of keys from minecraft, and in any area that isnt a boss zone, you can build freely. Most objects, once placed, will happily hover (even furniture) until broken manually. There are a handful of objects that will break when the block theyre attached to is broken, such as plants, lights, and doors. While the game doesnt offer as much variety as Minecraft does for building blocks and decorations, there's plenty to build something interesting and unique.

[h1]Endgame[/h1]
The endgame of Portal Knights is literally building your house/castle/whatever, hunting recipes and vanity items, or farming [spoiler]The Gate dungeon[/spoiler] for Energy Crystals for top tier equipment, bosses, hardmode bosses (challenging even with overpowered builds), or world events. Given that only players you allow into your world will ever see your house, thats basically for showing off to your friends or amusing yourself (which in itself isn't neccesarilty bad). While not entirely surprising, how long this lasts for you depends on how much you enjoy the building aspect of the game, and combat as a whole. [spoiler]Once you figure out a tactic for the hardmode bossfights, they tend to go really easily unless you make a judgement call mistake.[/spoiler]

Upvote absolutely.

SUMMARY: A straightforward and sincere "Fantasy RPG Minecraft" game with a lot of charm that's easy to pick up.  Tthe game focuses well on the core ideas - building, crafting, monster-fighting, and of course dressing fashionably, with more than enough surprises to take it farther.  A good choice if you're into the idea, and a relaxing game.

Portal Knights is exactly what it looks like - Minecraft meets Fantasy RPG with multiplayer options.  There's monster-fighting, crafting, building, questing, and so on.  You can guess how it works - travel to lands, get resources, make cool equipment, build a base, travel to more lands, build more equipment, all the while fighting monsters and taking quests.

Since the way the game plays is obvious, let's look at it in detail.

INTERFACE AND CONTROLS: These mostly work, and are easy to pick up.  It's clear the designers learned their lessons looking at other games, and there's some smart choices in options, changing views, and so on.
- The Camera and insta-lock (optional) can be annoying and distracting and don't work with all environments.  Customize controls accordingly.

SETTING: The game is set on shattered worlds, islands floating in the sky, the remnants of a terrible disaster.  This means that everyone gets to wander their own procedural sky-islands, so everyone plays the same game with different generated environments (with the same events).  This is pretty neat, and you can set parameters for your game "universe" and even jump between them.
- Some procedural islands can be deathtraps or require careful navigation.

PLOT: The game's core idea is interesting, and there are a few neat moments (the endgame video is pretty neat).
- VERY little is done with the plot or characters, which is disappointing for such a neat idea.

QUESTS: Are mostly straightforward and are ways to get more stuff.  Most dungeons and quests are "bite-sized" so you can play in 30 minutes or less.
- Quests aren't that innovative (though some dungeon layouts are fun).

CHARACTER PROGRESSION: Is pretty simple, you level up by fighting monsters and doing quests.  Experience unlocks attributes and class-specific abilities.  Otherwise everything is done by crafting armor, weapons, and skills and chosing what to use  - and there are few class restrictions, meaning you can make some interesting mixes of equipment and abilities.  A real strong point.

GAME PROGRESSION: You leap from island to island, collecting special shards that let you activate portals to go to new lands - which you have to find, adding to the challenge.  Also random events may spawn temporary portals!

RESOURCE GATHERING:  Prepare to do a lot of mining, lumberjacking, and cultivating.  For real success you'll need to put some effort into these so you've got all the tools and potions and structures you need.  As an added bit of strategy, some farming is environment-restricted, so if you want to make everything, you need to plan.
- Gathering is near-unavoidable.  So if you don't like it, sorry.

CRAFTING: Crafting goes pretty deep.  You need to build and upgrade various structures to make equipment, collect resources, get blueprints, and more.  Equipment has different traits that matter to your game choices.  This also synergizes with opening up new islands and finding special events.  If you don't want to craft you can find or buy equipment and resources, which is nice, but to go max you need to do it yourself.

BUILDING: Building  Minecraft-like, with some (mostly) helpful targeting.  You can build everywhere (which helps with some challenges), and early in the game can get private sky islands to build on.  You get a variety of decorations and building enhancements, many of which are colorful as well as useful, so you can make very charming structures.  A really nice touch is that many characters can be recruited, so soon your own little homestead/lodge/whatever can have its own population, making it a one-stop shop.
- Building doesn't innovate and is unavoidable to an extent, so if you don't like building - sorry.

COMBAT: Combat is mostly a simple case of using the best equipment, some spells, and consumables - then learning enemy patterns.  Smart play lets you overcome low levels and bad equipment.  It's not innovative, but is accessible.
- As noted, the camera can be a pain so customize carefully.

GRAPHICS AND PRESENTATION: The game is very colorful and charming, and has an endearing quality.

CHALLENGE: The game's challenge really depends on your experience and willingness to grind and craft.  If you're an old hand you can probably handle the core game pretty easily.  On the other hand this is idea for newcomers who can get used to the game.  Note some events and bosses can really spike the difficulty, so don't get complacent.
- Challenge might not be enough for some players, and the spikes/variances can surprise you.

EXTRAS: One of the best part of the game is that there are extras, events, and more that happen - with time limits.  Logging in may result in fun time limited random events and so on, which adds a lot to the game.
- End-game content at this time is just a few bosses, one dungeon, and some extended quests.

MULTIPLAYER: Is pretty functional.  You can find open worlds, open your own worlds, and share with friends.  Creative mode even lets you build places for others to explore, with some limtis - yes there's an entire "build your own environment" sub-element.
- Multiplayer networking has had moments of being spotty.  Hopefully that's being adressed.

ENTERTAINMENT: The game is fun, period. It's clear real joy went into making this.  It may not be your kind of fun, but its clear the people making it had a target and hit it.

So would I reccomend it?
* If the description fits, its probably for you.  This is one of those games that you sorta "know" fits you.  If you think you may like it, you'll like it - this was my case, where I debated it on and off, then got it and loved it.
* If you want a relaxing RPG/crafting experience.  It's pretty chill. This is a game you can have fun with.
* If you want an RPG that has a lot to do but doesn't "push" you too hard.
* It's a good game to play with a less experienced but creative gamer or a party.

Overall, a sincere and fun effort.  It doesn't break much new ground, it has some flaws, but it delivers a lot of fun things to do if you like the RPG/Minecraft fusion idea, and it may just surprise you.

I have only played about an hour and a half of the game, but from what I can tell, there isn't much too it.

You start out on an abysmally small floating island, and are presented three quests to complete in order to teach you the basics of the game. Make a pick axe, kill some mobs, create a portal.

The point of the game is to go to all the worlds and then kill the boss at the end, I guess. The systems in the game are very clunky and strange. Anyway, to the nitty gritty.

  [h1] The Good [/h1]

1. The game is very pretty and is visually impressive, for what it's worth.
2. The crafting holds promise for the future, but there is really no point to it other than upgrade your equipment and forget about it.
3. You can customize your character differently, so there's that.
4. There are 3 different classes, I'll touch on this later.
5. Can play first person or in third person mode, which is really nice option.

 [h1] The Bad [/h1]

-- [u] Combat [/u]--

1. Auto Targeting is awful. It is a Tab-Targeting oriented combat, which doesn't really work out very well. 
2. Can't move while attacking. You swing your sword/axe/mace and it moves you toward your targeted enemy a small distance, hopefully so you stay within hit radius.
3. Camera Locks in combat, and it's very bad. It zooms in and goes into a letterbox mode.
4. Automatic. You just right click and wait for the enemies lifebar to go away.
5. Clunky mechanics. You can't Evade attacks midswing, and must be standing stationary in order to execute an Evade.
6. You cannot attack a mob on a block higher or lower than you in melee. 



Now, the combat could be worse, but it's also nothing special. It's extremely basic and feels very automated to the extent where you literally just hold Left Click and drink a potion once in a while.

-- [u] Exploration/Sandbox [/u]--

1. Nonexistant. The "Worlds" you go to are nothing more than tiny floating islands. By tiny, I mean depressingly tiny. Small enough to where you can explore the entire thing in 3 minutes. 
2. Uninspired. The worlds are all disconnected and isntanced chunks of land. There is no reason at all to ever stop and build, because you will leave the island in 7 minutes and be on your way. 
3. Linear. There is no need explore anything, you kill some mobs, get your portal made and then leave the island. There is nothing noteworthy to find and it leaves the adventure feeling dead and bland.
4. The entire world is made the same every time. Same mob spawns, same layout, everything.
5. This game feels like the sandbox was an afterthought. You could play the entire game without ever crafting or building anything other than a crafting table.


 -- [u] Other [/u] --

1. You cannot allocate your stat points when you level up manually, they are automatically allocated, and the Skill Talents are boring and very dry.
2. The inventory/menu is tragic. 
3. You cannot drop items or trade items. The only way to give another player an item is to put it in a chest for them to pick it up. 
4. No Sprint/Run ability. Can't jump in combat, can't look around in combat.

This game leaves much to be desired. 

[h1] Suggestions [/h1]

[u] Add purpose [/u]

In order to progress to the next world, require you to perform a task or defeat a mob, complete a puzzle, something in order for you to feel you are progressing towards something, not just killing some mobs to get your portal crystals and leave. 

 [u] Seemless World [/u] 

No portals. At all. The system is dumb and doesn't make sense in a sandbox game. Sandbox games are supposed to be an open world, not a series of instanced islands (extremely small islands, at that). Give a reason to build a base and crafting station. Perhaps create a "Peace Zone," that instead of "Portal Crystals" you get "Purity Crystals" that you can create a beacon of sorts to cause mobs not to spawn in X radius, and allows you to build Peace Zone only items, such as beds to spawn in or teleport to, crafting stations to upgrade armor and weapons, things of that nature.  

The game desperately needs a large seemless environment, it's the biggest hinderance to the game in my opinion. I had little to know satisfaction running from island to island mindlessly killing mobs for portal crystals. It's a shame, because the game could be great.

[u] Customization [/u] 

Allow custom stat allocation. Let me put my points where I want them. There needs to be many more Skill Traits, and better ones too. Seriously, 30% increased mining speed? 15% Reduced Mining Durability damage? What the actual hell? Where is the "build your own story" part of the game at? You aren't given [i]any[/i] tools to do this with. There are no quests other than the first 3 on the first world that is more of a .readme file.

[u] Action Combat [/u] 

Remove the Tab Targeting system entirely. You should not be tab targeting in an action combat game, it should be hitbox swing radius based. You should be able to cancel attacks with dodge roll, and be able to RUN ffs. Enemies are only dangerous in large packs, and melee is horrifically imbalanced and bad. Warriors are useless. 

There is a lot of things I could suggest, but it's 6am and I need to go to bed.

All in all I feel very ripped off. This game should not have the Sandbox, Survival, Crafting, or Building tags. There is literally not a single Survival based element in the entire game, other than "don't take too much damage because you'll die."

It is in early access, but I feel that if they don't change a vast majority of the games systems, it won't do well. In its current state it is barely enjoyable. It was good for the first 40 minutes until I realized that there is no point in the game and nothing felt rewarding or exciting. 

Do I recommend this game? No. Absolutely not. There are many other great voxel sandbox games out there to play. 

[h1] Overall rating [/h1]
 [b] 4/10 [/b]

Portal Knights has so successfully blended building with FUN action/adventure quest lines that I honestly cannot find a good replacement. My only drawbacks really are a) it is a bit cute-looking b) some quests/worlds get a little repetitive, as is the bane with most games honestly, and c) no cross-platform play (yet?...). I will have to keep an eye on this publisher to see if they produce some games that age with their audience.  In a few years they could come out with something really amazing for the older crowd.  Till then, I have no shame goofing around on here making castles and killing dragons.

Only recently realized I never wrote a review for Portal knights and consider it my duty regarding how much time I spent in that beautiful world.

The first thing that caught my eye about it was the adorable graphic and the RPG elements. Gears with stats, levels, different classes and real time combat. I ll say upfront that all these things are rather basic and certainly not the meat of the game but it was what introduce me in the first place.

It looks better then Minecraft also a factor because MC is just plain ugly to me and the mean reason why I never played it. This seemed to be Minecraft with a touch of its own. And its really the visual presentation that makes it stand out. The overall world looks very rough due to the size of the building blocks but there are so many assets, statues, doors, interior etc that just looks amazing and brings a place to life. Dungeons or caves look definitely creepy and the overall map design gave me a ton of squeemish moments when I tried to jump a ledge or reach a higher point.

There are quests that help you to get into features and mechanics but overall its a sandbox take with gated content meaning you have to work up your way to reach higher level maps. Bring up your level and your gear in order to survive obstacles and unlock more and more options.

Very quickly you start to spend time on small "projects" that you spotted somewhere and tried to create for your own. A small hut, a tower, a garden you name it. And once you start you realize that the whole game is designed to support your every creative wish. You can easily lose HOURS just trying out building material and then once you spent 10 hours on that dream mansion of yours you enter a new map, find a new building block and tear down the whole thing and start from scratch because you think crystal walls look amazing.

Make no mistake....building a house yourself is tedious work. People hype over the end result but try mounting 4 walls, each 200 blocks strong...which you need to GET first (I razed countless pregenerated castles to the ground in order to get those runestone blocks) and you quickly figure out that the last hour of your life was wasted on placing pixel blocks in a straight line.

Welcome to the Minecraft-syndrome ^^

Details become absolutely important. You get caught in a loop where you have to tear out whole sections because ONE SINGLE BLOCK "aint right" and you realize how important planning is. So you continue playing Portal Knights even tho you dont play it. All those lunch breaks huddled over pieces of paper scribbling down the "next project" obsessing over size, metrics, locations, interio design....and then you come back home, boot up the game and try to make it a reality.

My wife caught me obsessively hacking away at ore and was wondering bout what I did. I showed her my half-assemlbed wood block house and she "wanted to get in on the action". 

Player 2 enters the game.

Seriously....leveling up and growing stronger as a character is just a side activity for us. We leveled up in order to farm stuff easier. We went through the quests because its a welcome distraction at times but we always booted the game up to build something.

And it really doesnt take much to trigger another Portal Knight episode.

A new class and we start out from scratch. A new map with new stuff to look at and we have to "update" all our projects. We made a cruise and came home only to replicate the ship we toured on. Spent a weekend in the wilderness....yep...you guessed it....we NEED to build that lodge in the game.

We are still building on a mega project. A gigantic castle out of Obsidian with lava stone edges. It has countless bedrooms and baths, comes with 4 corner towers, a personal dungeon and swimming pool. And building the foundation is just the start. Oftentimes we spent whole evenings just getting furniture and moving stuff around in order to find the "perfect setup".

So depending on what you look for Portal Knights definitely can provide you with endless hours of entertainment. Enemies are simple on their own but engage multiple foes at once and things become frantic. Simple changes in skills and gear can result in massive performance differences. Portal Knights is a game that easily allows you to lose yourself in the details.

And the devs have been great over the years. The game got support, a great community and we received tons of free stuff over the years. It does have DLCs for money and its arguable if those DLCs actually are worth the asking prize but hell....this game deserves some recognition from time to time.

If you want a roleplaying game then PK isnt for you. Its too shallow, too limited and too short to compete against actual RPG games. But if you are into creative side of games and look for a little more progression among mindlessly building stuff then this is a dream come true.

11/10 easily ^^

In an ideal world, what could we add to this game to make it worthwhile? Functional buildings, AI for mobs and a lifelike world design.

The strength of a voxel game is that it allows players to create interesting structures.

In Portal Knights, building is placing blocks. That's it. There is nothing to build which would be useful (apart from stacking blocks to reach higher places).
There is no functionality, like building a shelter, building traps or any other kind of structure which grants you a strategic advantage.
Well, building is not needed because enemies have their 5m attack radius and retreat after you move a bit away, just to stand on the same spot again.
AI is basically non-existing in this game.
Base building in non-voxel games like 'The Forest' is extremely limiting in comparison but much more rewarding.

In addition, the setup with these numerous but small islands may be a mistake. They are not diverse enough to keep up the anticipation of exploring.
Larger interesting and hand crafted structures serving as settings for a quest-chain with significance beyond mere resource gathering and xp farming, are hard to squeeze into these micro worlds.

Portal Knights completely lacks scope and depth. There is pretty much no reason to play this game.

In theory, Portal Knights is a Minecraft clone with the addition of (boring) fetch quests. You travel through a series of worlds by finding portals. Each world has different resources for you to harvest, so you'll often need to travel among several worlds to collect everything you need. You can setup a base in any or all worlds you travel to, but it makes the most sense to declare one world as your Home world and setup a single base there.  Either way, you'll still be travelling back and forth between several worlds to collect the specific resources you need for the next tier of items.

The whole point of the game, from what I can tell, is to collect items in order to craft better items which help you collect more items faster and craft even more items... It's just an endless cycle of resource harvesting and crafting with no meaningful end goal.  If the resource harvesting were enjoyable, then the means would be acceptable, but turns out harvesting for the sake of harvesting is dreadfully boring.  The 3+ boss fights are made easier if you have higher-level gear, but who cares!? The bosses are just meaningless fights you must encounter at specific points before you can advance. Plus, the penalty for dying is the loss of some coins (which serve no useful purpose), so nothing is lost if you face a boss too soon and die a lot in the process.

Very few NPCs serve any purpose, but occasionally you will find one that runs a store or offers a quest. I have yet to see a point to the coins you collect as all shopkeepers sell useless garbage (like seeds or pets) that you can easily collect in any number of worlds. The handful of random quests you encounter periodically throughout the various worlds nearly all require you to find or craft a certain item and bring it back to the NPC. A few will have you kill X number of an enemy type. The easiest way to finish the item quests is to just warp back to your home base, craft the item, and bring it back to the NPC... but there's a problem. The Universe map doesn't tell you which quests you have active in each world, so it's impossible to track your quest status in game unless you travel to each and every world to manually check for a quest. Once you're in the right world you then need to hunt down the NPC who gave you the quest, because there is no indication to tell you where to go.

The game is downright boring in solo, so multiplayer is a must, but it has a terrible multiplayer setup. The Universe map is linked to a player's character, so if you join someone else's multiplayer game, the only progress you will retain is your character's level and current inventory. Any portals you open in another player's Universe will not transfer back to your character's Universe. This means if you start a game with friends, you will never be able to play solo without them unless you want to restart the exploration process.  Considering the worlds fail to offer anything unique, therefore providing no reason to ever revisit them (except resource gathering), the idea of having to restart is unacceptable.  This game desperately needs a way to setup a dedicated server, otherwise the multiplayer likely won't survive.

Mechanically, I think the game is okay. There are 3 different classes, each with its own specialty and gear.  The graphics are gorgeous, the audio tracks are fantastic, the combat is more or less good, but the complete lack of meaningful activities is unforgivable.  What activities are present are so shallow that they really don't offer anything fun to come back to.  This game may actually be redeemable if the developers decide to add any meaningful content, but I doubt that will happen anytime soon. At a minimum, the following must be addressed:

* There are not enough boss fights.
* There are not enough enemy varieties (though I am thankful to see that while enemies are repeated, they do at least have different strengths/weaknesses in each world.)
* There are not enough quest-granting NPCs.
* There are too many crafting quests (those that just require you to build a weapon and give it to the NPC).
* Active quests need to be visible from the Universe map, not just within the world that has the quest.
* There are not enough merchant NPCs.
* Merchants and coins are useless (the few Merchants I encounter never have anything worth purchasing).
* Inventory size should be expandable.
* Each world should be distinctly unique in one or more noteworthy aspects.

Summary: 
A jack of all trades but master of none, Portal Knights is an RPG-inspired Minecraft clone/looting simulator set in a post-fracture world (a collection of level based sandboxes), a game with great intention but poor execution.

[b]Gameplay[/b]
The gameplay mostly consists of looting with a moderate emphasis on leveling your character. While there is a combat system, it isn't anything terribly complex or challenging, as any fight considered "hard" is more about not dying/spending prolonged hours chipping at a wall. 
There exists a few elements unique to the class you choose (3 base game 2 dlc) which differ the gameplay slightly, but there's obvious imbalances in how good they are (thus making it unfun to play certain classes). 
Many of the RPG elements are stock standard, and in some cases, substandard to what you might find even on an RPGMaker game, such as the rudimentary questing system and primitive gameplay progression. It feels like the foundation for a deeper system that was rushed to completion and not fleshed out for sake of time or perhaps budget.

The second element one might notice about this game is the blocks, but don't be fooled! Building takes absolute bottom priority in the game aside from placing 6 portal stones per gate (of which a level may have 3 gates at most) to progress to the next level. I only noted a few quests involving building, most of which were simple craft-then-place jobs for gimmick blocks. Other than this, the game might as well not even have blocks considering how little you actually need to use them. The framework is there for fun gameplay, but it isn't used.

[b]Achievements[/b]
As with most games, the achievements are fairly stock standard progression-based participation medals, but there are a few standout entries, mostly being combat challenges. The most annoying/time consuming achievement would be completing 200 event quests, events that happen every 5 minutes or so, forcing the player to either cheese the achievement or waste many hours waiting for them to pop up.

[b]Story[/b]
The story concept isn't terrible, in fact, it sets up a great framework for an RPG world. The issue lay within how little it's fleshed out, how little you feel the story has an impact on the world (besides an excuse for level-based worlds), and how 1 dimensional it is. You get some tidbits here and there about the lore, but it feels completely lackluster for an RPG game. Were the dialogue system or NPCs to be improved, it could pave the way for better immersion.

[b]Hate[/b]
You can find most of my discontent peppered throughout the review, but I feel it's mostly directed at the combat and building; it disregards the principle of Chekhov's gun (if you write a story with gun on the wall, use it) wherein the tools are there, but they aren't being used. This wouldn't be a problem though, were modding supported for the game, which it is not (and which is why this game is much inferior to other Minecraft clones and why no new content will be introduced to the game long term).
The combat and building aside, many elements of the game (like the NPCs) feel like a ghost of an idea, something perceptible but not tangible within the game, like a house frame with no walls. 

Unfinished but playable is the best way I can describe Portal Knights.

So after playing about 14 hours of this game, I can say I have a really good feel of this game.  I am very mixed on it.  The game is like  a mix of Zelda, Minecraft, and harvest moon.

Multiplayer:
This works OK.  My biggest issues is that everyone has to be in the same portal as the host of the game.  This is really annoying when trying to get mats from different portals.  The only fix we have come up with (my three friends who played 14 hours with me) is that each person who needs different mats leaves the game and goes into their own game to farm. Once they have the stuff they need they can then come back and join the host in their "main server".  

Visuals:
The game is visually appealing. It runs very well in 1080p, but anything above that it starts doesn't translate properly.  Also has problems with alt tabbing out.  The screen goes to windows screen and cannot change unless you completely reload the game.  I also had some friends who couldn't even play the game because the graphics were stuttering or broken. The game needs major optimization.

Combat:
The battles and the monsters are pretty awesome.  I like the range of weapons you can use and how the combat flows. By weapon of choice by far is the bow and the sword.  The bow is good for long range and not taking a lot of damage.  The sword will make quick  work of a group of monsters. The diversity of the monsters is pretty cool changing from day to night.  I would like to see more.

Portals:
Each portal is pretty cool. They change in vegetation and the monster that inhabitants them.  They also seem to get progressively bigger as you go through each portal with is cool. The first portal is my base and house I have built up.  I would like to see this area changed so it is bigger.  Right now it is pretty small and if you get a number of farms going you run out of space quick.  I have had to clear and add extra blocks to the outside of the portal zone areas to fit stuff.

Controls:
I use a piece of software and have mapped my controller to play the game. I don't know why they haven't mapped a controller to the game.  It works perfectly with controller. 

Action bar:
I have a love hate with the action bar.  I am not sure why potions or sharpening stones when placed on your action bar become circles??? I can select them when scrolling through with my mouse or using my quick key scrolls on my triggers that I have mapped on my xbox controller. They need to get rid of this.  It also took my buddies and I about 4-5 hours of game play before we figured out you have to have your weapon selected and click the hot key that you have your sharpening stones on to repair it.  We tried finding this information on the internet with no luck.  They need to make this more aware of how to do this or change how this mechanic works.

Building:
I love the range of the pickaxe.  One of my biggest gripes with Minecraft is that your hit box was so short. This game makes it very easy to mine/clear stuff that is far away or above your head.  Keep this up! It is very easy to build and create the different items you need to do this.  I have so far built a house and a castle.

Farming:
Farming works awesome in this game.  You can plant seeds and within an hour they are ready to be harvest. I have a beautiful garden going by my house that I have collected seeds from all the different portals.  My favourite are the cool big mushrooms.  The only other thing I would like to see is possibly pets or animals?  I don't know how you would integrate  them in the game.  Maybe as mounts or as a way to clear/collect stuff?  Maybe unleash a goat in your garden to collect all your cotton :)

Mining:
Mining works pretty good.  The only gripe I have with mining is that some of the items you can use to do special mining are junk. I keep going back to my copper pickaxe.  It mines the best and does the best job all around.  The mining claw is junk and the drill is junk.  It would be cool if the drill took out 8-10 blocks at a time for clearing big areas, but it doesn't.  The claw also doesn't seem to really have any big benefit over the copper pickaxe.  

Crafting:
Crafting is very easy to use. You can see what mats you need and get the gear going. The only thing I would really like to see is enchant able or magical gear.

Dungeons, spelunking, and Bosses:
This is my biggest gripe. My friends and I were so excited when exploring dungeons and caves. Nothing was more of a letdown when getting to the bottom of a cave and breaking open a cache. What's in the cache you ask? Gold? Treasures? New items or equipment?  NOPE.  You got some potions and some mats that you can easily farm by yourself.  They need to change this greatly.  There is literally no point to exploring caves, spelunking, or beating bosses.  They need to change this.  They need to add more mini bosses that are harder to beat and that have a chance of dropping something that is RARE.  Not a potion of health or mana (which I rarely even use) or some mats that are easily collected by yourself.  

Conclusion
The biggest draw to the game is the building/farming  and somewhat crafting side at this point. I have enjoyed those so far, but I find based on what they currently have , it will get old quick. The monsters and boss loots need to be beefed up and better gear drops need to be added.  Also gear needs to be upgraded a bit more.  It needs to be enchantable and a bit more variety to it.  Gemming would be a pretty cool feature.
The official website says it is cross platform but the game is not cross platform
